independent_interpretation: A point particle of mass m moves with constant rectilinear velocity v along the line y = d (d > 0) in the xy-plane. We determine the magnitude and time-dependence of the particle's angular momentum with respect to the origin O.
governing_principles: Vector Definition of Particle Angular Momentum (L = r x p)
Geometric Formulation of Angular Momentum (|L| = p * r_perp)
Angular Momentum Theorem (dL/dt = tau_ext = r x F_ext)
independent_solution_steps: Step 1: Set up the particle position vector relative to the origin O in Cartesian coordinates: r(t) = x(t) i + d j.
Step 2: Express the momentum vector: Since velocity is constant along the line y = d, v = v i, giving p = m v i.
Step 3: Evaluate the cross product: L = r x p = (x i + d j) x (m v i) = x m v (i x i) + d m v (j x i) = - m v d k.
Step 4: Take the magnitude: |L| = m v d. Notice that the x-coordinate drops out entirely because the perpendicular distance from O to the trajectory line is invariant (r_perp = d).
Step 5: Check dynamic conservation: Since v is constant, net force F = m dv/dt = 0, which means net torque tau = r x F = 0. Therefore, dL/dt = 0, proving L is strictly conserved for all time.

Step 6: Audit distractors: Option A is based on the misconception that rectilinear motion implies zero angular momentum; Option B confuses radial distance r = sqrt(x^2+d^2) with lever arm r_perp; Option D falsely claims angular position changes cause oscillation in L.
notes: First-principles evaluation confirms |L| = m v d is strictly constant for all time. Option C is unique and correct. All distractors are invalid.
